stem.text: The green-eyed tree-frog, Litoria genimaculata, lives in tropical rainforests in Australia. Around 5 million years ago, the tree-frog population split into northern (N) and southern (S) populations that were separated by a dry area with no rainforest.
6500 years ago, the N and S tree-frog populations came into contact again as a warmer climate allowed rainforest to grow again in the area between the N and S populations.
Figure 3.1 is a map showing an area, labelled the contact zone, where N and S populations of tree-frog currently come into contact.

stem.alt: Map of northern and southern green-eyed tree-frog populations and their contact zone near the Barron River.

stem.text: N tree-frogs and S tree-frogs can be distinguished by genetic techniques.
Outline the genetic techniques that could be used to distinguish between N and S tree-frog DNA.

database / bioinformatics, to, compare / analyse, sequences of, (DNA) bases / nucleotides ;

explanation.text: DNA differences can be detected by amplifying a selected region and comparing fragment patterns or sequences. PCR increases the amount available; electrophoresis separates fragments by length.

Explain how a difference in the DNA would become distinguishable.

stem.text: Explain how a period of geographical separation, such as the one that occurred between the N and S tree-frog populations, can eventually lead to speciation.

points.text: idea of no contact so, reproductive isolation / no gene flow (between populations) ;
so can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring ;

explanation.text: Geographical isolation restricts gene flow. Different mutations, selection pressures and drift can then cause divergence until reproductive isolation persists even after contact is restored.

reasoningChain: Explain the interruption of gene flow.
Trace genetic divergence to reproductive isolation.

stem.text: Scientists were interested in tree-frogs in the contact zone.

items: In the wild, S female tree-frogs are strongly attracted to the mating call of S male tree-frogs but are not attracted to the mating call of N male tree-frogs.
In the laboratory, when an S female tree-frog is mated with a male N tree-frog, none of the fertilised eggs develop into offspring.

stem.text: Suggest, with reasons, what these observations show about speciation between N tree-frogs and S tree-frogs.

points.text: they are now different species / speciation has taken place ;
(when S female and N male mate) offspring not produced / (fertilised) eggs are not viable ;

markScheme.note: Point n follows the order of the transcribed marking points; table rows or source labels such as 3a and 3b retain their original wording.

explanation.text: The observations test two separate barriers: mate recognition before fertilisation and failure of hybrid development after fertilisation. Together they support reproductive isolation despite renewed geographical contact.

reasoningChain: Use the mating-call observation for a behavioural barrier.
Use failure of fertilised eggs to develop for a postzygotic barrier.

stem.text: There is a large variation in body length within the population of N tree-frogs and within the population of S tree-frogs.
Describe the factors that interact to cause this variation in body length.

points.text: diet / food (availability) / competition for food / nutrients / temperature / disease ;

explanation.text: Body length can reflect the combined effects of many loci and environmental conditions such as food availability. The same genotype may produce different lengths in different environments.

reasoningChain: Explain an environmental influence and its interaction with genotype.
